transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, um… I guess what finally made me come in is work. I’m a buyer, so I’m always dealing with purchase numbers, vendor quotes, launch quantities, that kind of stuff, and lately I just cannot get past this feeling that people are watching what I buy or tracking it somehow. Like not just normal tracking in the system—more like people at work, and even some of the vendors, are messing with the launch numbers so that when everything gets reviewed it makes me look stupid or like I don’t know what I’m doing.

And I know how that sounds, because my supervisor has sat down with me and pulled up reports and tried to show me, like, “Look, the numbers don’t prove that,” or “This is just how the launch was entered,” but it doesn’t really settle it for me. I’ll look at it and for a minute I’ll think maybe I’m overreacting, but then I start noticing little things again, like changes in timing or the way someone phrases an email, and it feels connected.

So… yeah. I’m here because I can’t shake it, and it’s starting to really get to me.
How long have you been feeling this way—do you remember when you first started noticing these suspicions about your coworkers and vendors?

Um… I think it’s been about ten months, give or take. It’s hard to pin down the exact start because at first it wasn’t like, “Oh, this is a thing now.” It was more like I noticed one or two things that felt off, and I kept telling myself maybe I was just stressed or reading into it.

But if I’m being honest, the suspicions about coworkers and vendors have been there for around ten months now. And the voice—like, that started around that same stretch of time too. It’s not something that just happened last week or anything. It’s been long enough that it feels like it’s kind of built into how I’m going through my day now, which is part of why I finally came in.
You mentioned a 'voice'—can you tell me more about that? Do you actually hear it as a sound, like someone speaking out loud, or is it more like a thought in your head?

Yeah… it’s more like I actually hear it, not just me thinking it. I mean, I know thoughts can be loud sometimes, and I’ve tried to tell myself maybe it’s just stress or my brain kind of talking to itself, but this feels different.

It’ll happen when I’m in the stockroom sometimes, like if I’m moving boxes or checking items, and I’ll hear this man’s voice like it’s coming from right behind me. Not inside my head exactly—more like someone standing close, over my shoulder. It’ll say things like, “Move faster, Scott,” or it’ll kind of laugh, like it’s making fun of what I picked or the quantities I chose. And I’ll turn around because it feels that real, like I’m expecting someone to be there, but nobody is.

It’s happened driving back from vendor meetings too, which really bothers me because I’ll be in the car alone and hear it like it’s behind me, and for a second I’ll look in the mirror or glance around even though I know there shouldn’t be anyone there. It’s not constant every minute, but when it happens it feels like a sound, not just a thought.

Over these past ten months, have you noticed any changes in your ability to keep up with daily responsibilities—like your motivation, energy, or interest in things you used to enjoy, or how you're managing personal care and relationships?

Yeah… definitely. I mean, I wish I could say it’s only bothering me in my head, but it’s not. My job has taken a real hit, honestly.

I’ve missed buying deadlines, which is not really something you can just shrug off in my role because if I miss a cutoff, it affects launch quantities and what stores actually have on hand. And I’ve messed up vendor relationships too, because I’ll get suspicious or worked up and then I’ll send emails that are too intense, or I’ll delay responding because I’m trying to figure out what they “really” mean, and then things get strained. A couple vendors have gone around me to my supervisor, which was embarrassing.

And then there were some purchasing calls I made that were… impulsive, I guess. At the time I felt like I had to act fast, like if I didn’t make the buy right then something would get twisted or used against me. But looking back, or at least when my supervisor went through it with me, some of it didn’t make much sense. I got formally warned over it, which scared me because I’ve always been pretty good at my job. Like, I may not have a fancy degree, but I know the work, or I thought I did.

Outside of work, I’ve kind of disappeared from people. I used to go to gallery nights with friends, and we’d do volleyball weekends, and I actually liked having those things on the calendar. Lately I just don’t show up. Sometimes I tell myself I’m too tired or I need to catch up on work stuff, but really I just don’t feel like being around everyone, and then it gets harder to explain why I’ve been gone, so I stay gone. It’s made everything feel smaller, I guess.

During these past ten months, have there been times when you also felt persistently very sad, hopeless, or lost interest in almost everything, or alternatively felt unusually elated, energetic, or 'high'—separate from the suspicious feelings and the voice?

Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t say it’s only sadness, exactly. There are definitely stretches where I feel… almost lifted up, like everything is suddenly possible and the whole city is kind of opening up for me. Like I’ll be walking to work or looking at vendor lists or even just riding the train, and it feels like there’s this big opportunity everywhere, like I can see connections other people are missing.

And when I’m in that kind of state, I feel more energized, more sure of myself. Not just “in a good mood,” but like I’m supposed to move fast and make things happen. And that can feel good at first, honestly. It feels like I’m finally not stuck.

But then if someone questions me—like if my supervisor asks why I placed a purchase order a certain way, or a vendor tells me to slow down, or even someone just pushes back a little—I snap way harder than I mean to. I get irritated really fast, like they’re blocking something important or trying to make me smaller. And afterward I can tell I came off too intense, but in the moment it feels completely justified. So yeah, there have been those elevated, charged-up stretches, and they come with this irritability that gets me into trouble.

Thinking about the times when you're NOT feeling that elevated, energized state—during your more normal or even-keeled stretches—do you still hear the voice or have those suspicious feelings about coworkers and vendors?

Yeah… that’s the part that makes it harder for me to explain away, honestly. Because it’s not only when I’m in that really charged-up state.

There was a stretch where I was calmer—like, I was sleeping more normally, I wasn’t feeling like I had to outrun the whole market or make every decision immediately. I wasn’t walking around with that same “everything is connected and I have to act now” feeling. But even then, for a few weeks, I still had this belief that people were tracking my buys. Like coworkers or vendors were watching what I ordered, comparing it, maybe keeping notes on it or using it somehow.

And the voice was still happening too. I remember being in the stockroom during that period and hearing it again, that same man’s voice, like it was right there behind me. So… yeah, even when my mood wasn’t all revved up, the suspicious stuff and the voice didn’t completely go away.

During this past ten months, roughly how much of the total time have you had these mood episodes—either the elevated, energized stretches or any low periods—compared to how much time you've spent in a more even, normal mood?

Looking back at it… I think most of the time has been those wired stretches, or at least the irritable, keyed-up version of them. Like not necessarily happy the whole time, but moving too fast, working too much, feeling overly sure I was right, and getting really hard to slow down.

There were calmer periods in between, yeah, where I felt more like I could breathe and wasn’t pushing everything so intensely. But those felt shorter. If I’m being honest, the bigger chunk of the last ten months has been me being revved up, overconfident, overworking, or getting angry when people tried to question me. The normal stretches were more like breaks in between, not the main thing.
During these past ten months, have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or new medications/supplements, or been diagnosed with any medical conditions like thyroid problems?

Um… I don’t really know. I mean, nothing that jumps out to me as, like, “this started after I took something,” if that’s what you mean.

I’m not great at keeping track of that kind of thing, honestly. I haven’t been sitting down and making a list of every drink or pill or anything. I don’t think there’s been some big new medical thing I was told about, like… no one has sat me down and said, “You have a thyroid problem,” or anything like that. At least not that I know of.

As far as new medications or supplements, I don’t think I started anything major. I mean, I might take random stuff here and there if I’m tired or feel off, like normal over-the-counter things, but I’m not on some new treatment that I can point to. And with alcohol or drugs… I don’t really have a clear answer beyond saying I haven’t noticed a connection. I’m not trying to dodge it—I just don’t want to say something definite if I’m not sure.

inference.note: The description of distinct manic-like episodes (elevated mood, grandiosity, increased energy, irritability) occurring alongside persistent psychotic symptoms supports a mood component significant enough to consider schizoaffective disorder (F25.0), while the chronicity and prominence of delusions/hallucinations keep paranoid schizophrenia (F20.0) in play. F28 is now less likely given the clearer mood and psychotic symptom pattern.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (paranoid beliefs, voice) occur during periods when mood is normal—not elevated or depressed—to clarify if psychosis is independent of mood episodes (key for distinguishing schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder).
doctor.question: Thinking about the times when you're NOT feeling that elevated, energized state—during your more normal or even-keeled stretches—do you still hear the voice or have those suspicious feelings about coworkers and vendors?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: Even during a calmer stretch when I was sleeping more normally and not feeling like I was running the whole market, I still spent a few weeks believing people were tracking my buys and hearing the voice in the stockroom.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the voice and suspicious beliefs continued during even-keeled periods when the elevated, energized mood was not present.

patient.answer:
Yeah… that’s the part that makes it harder for me to explain away, honestly. Because it’s not only when I’m in that really charged-up state.

There was a stretch where I was calmer—like, I was sleeping more normally, I wasn’t feeling like I had to outrun the whole market or make every decision immediately. I wasn’t walking around with that same “everything is connected and I have to act now” feeling. But even then, for a few weeks, I still had this belief that people were tracking my buys. Like coworkers or vendors were watching what I ordered, comparing it, maybe keeping notes on it or using it somehow.

And the voice was still happening too. I remember being in the stockroom during that period and hearing it again, that same man’s voice, like it was right there behind me. So… yeah, even when my mood wasn’t all revved up, the suspicious stuff and the voice didn’t completely go away.

inference.note: Patient confirms psychotic symptoms (voice, paranoid delusions) persisted for weeks during euthymic/non-manic periods, supporting psychotic disorder with mood episodes (schizoaffective) rather than mood disorder alone. Need to clarify total proportion of time psychosis occurs without mood symptoms and duration relative to 10-month course to distinguish F25.0 from F20.0.

doctor.intent: Determine the total duration of psychotic symptoms (voice/suspicions) relative to mood episodes, to assess whether psychosis persists substantially outside mood episodes (favoring schizophrenia) or is mostly confined to mood episodes (favoring schizoaffective disorder)
doctor.question: During this past ten months, roughly how much of the total time have you had these mood episodes—either the elevated, energized stretches or any low periods—compared to how much time you've spent in a more even, normal mood?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, most of the time since this all started has been taken up by those wired or irritable stretches where I was overworking, overconfident, and hard to slow down, with only shorter calmer periods in between.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how much of the overall illness period was spent in mood episodes versus normal mood, which directly relates to whether manic mood episodes were present for the majority of the illness duration.

patient.answer:
Looking back at it… I think most of the time has been those wired stretches, or at least the irritable, keyed-up version of them. Like not necessarily happy the whole time, but moving too fast, working too much, feeling overly sure I was right, and getting really hard to slow down.

There were calmer periods in between, yeah, where I felt more like I could breathe and wasn’t pushing everything so intensely. But those felt shorter. If I’m being honest, the bigger chunk of the last ten months has been me being revved up, overconfident, overworking, or getting angry when people tried to question me. The normal stretches were more like breaks in between, not the main thing.

inference.note: The patient reports that mood episodes (manic/irritable, energized states) occupied the majority of the 10-month period, with psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations) persisting even during a distinct euthymic stretch of several weeks. This pattern—prominent, predominant mood symptoms coexisting with psychotic symptoms, plus psychotic symptoms present for a sustained period without mood symptoms—fits the ICD-10 criteria for schizoaffective disorder, manic type (F25.0), and argues against primary schizophrenia (F20.0), since in F20.0 mood symptoms would not dominate the clinical course to this degree.

doctor.intent: Rule out substance use or medical conditions that could account for the psychotic and mood symptoms
doctor.question: During these past ten months, have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or new medications/supplements, or been diagnosed with any medical conditions like thyroid problems?

target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking about alcohol or drug use, new medications/supplements, or medical conditions such as thyroid problems as possible causes; none of the provided symptom profile items cover substance use, medication effects, or general medical conditions.

patient.answer:
Um… I don’t really know. I mean, nothing that jumps out to me as, like, “this started after I took something,” if that’s what you mean.

I’m not great at keeping track of that kind of thing, honestly. I haven’t been sitting down and making a list of every drink or pill or anything. I don’t think there’s been some big new medical thing I was told about, like… no one has sat me down and said, “You have a thyroid problem,” or anything like that. At least not that I know of.

As far as new medications or supplements, I don’t think I started anything major. I mean, I might take random stuff here and there if I’m tired or feel off, like normal over-the-counter things, but I’m not on some new treatment that I can point to. And with alcohol or drugs… I don’t really have a clear answer beyond saying I haven’t noticed a connection. I’m not trying to dodge it—I just don’t want to say something definite if I’m not sure.

inference.note: Confirmed mood episodes (manic/irritable) occupy majority of the 10-month illness course, while psychotic symptoms (paranoid delusions, auditory hallucination) persisted during at least a few weeks without prominent mood symptoms, satisfying both the mood-majority and psychosis-without-mood criteria for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type. No substance or medical cause identified, further supporting this diagnosis and ruling out substance-induced or medical psychotic disorders.
